entries.proposition: Eligibility required a minimum convulsive seizure count in the 12 weeks before screening and in the prospective baseline.
entries.snippet: Participants were required to have had ≥12 convulsive seizures over 12 weeks before screening and at least four convulsive seizures per 28 days during the 4–6‐week screening period.

entries.proposition: The primary endpoint was the percentage change in convulsive seizure frequency per 28 days; the endpoint was agreed with epileptologists before start.
entries.snippet: The primary endpoints were percentage change from baseline in convulsive seizure frequency per 28 days in participants receiving soticlestat compared with placebo during the full treatment period

entries.proposition: Multiplicity was controlled by hierarchical gatekeeping; after a failed primary all later p-values are nominal.
entries.snippet: If a test was not statistically significant at a two‐sided 5% significance level, subsequent hypotheses were not tested, and any reported p‐values should be considered nominal (not adjusted for multiplicity).

entries.proposition: The phase 2 trial had reported a 50 percent placebo-adjusted median reduction in convulsive seizures in children with Dravet syndrome.
entries.snippet: demonstrated a statistically significant placebo‐adjusted median reduction in convulsive seizure frequency of 50.0% (95% confidence interval [CI] −74.2% to −24.7%, p = .0002).

entries.proposition: The phase 3 primary result was a 15.64 percent difference with p 0.061 over the full treatment period.
entries.snippet: The difference was a reduction of 15.64% (95% CI = −31.30 to .24, p = .061).
entries.anchor: Results, Effect on convulsive seizure frequency

entries.proposition: Positive outcomes cannot be declared for the key secondary endpoints because the primary missed.
entries.snippet: These key secondary endpoints showed nominal statistical significance, but because the primary endpoint did not reach statistical significance, positive outcomes cannot be declared for secondary endpoints.

entries.proposition: Clinician-rated global impression of non-seizure symptoms (alertness, communication, disruptive behaviour) did not differ between arms.
entries.snippet: No meaningful differences were observed between treatment groups in CGI‐I Non‐Seizure Symptoms (i.e., alertness, communication, disruptive behaviors; Figure 4F–H).

entries.proposition: The authors name a higher placebo response than in phase 2 and a more refractory population as contributors.
entries.snippet: Potential contributors to this narrowly missed statistical significance on the primary outcome are a higher placebo response than in the phase 2 study and a generally more refractory patient population

entries.proposition: The same Discussion says the miss is unlikely to be due to a high placebo response.
entries.snippet: Narrowly missed significance on the primary endpoints is unlikely to be due to a high placebo response, as the placebo rate was in line with clinical trials of other approved drugs for the treatment of DS.

entries.proposition: The SCN1A-positive subgroup analysis was exploratory and nominal, p 0.045.
entries.snippet: showed a nominally significant reduction from baseline in convulsive seizure frequency (p = .045) with soticlestat versus placebo.

entries.proposition: Post hoc, the most treatment-resistant quartile had an unfavourable estimate.
entries.snippet: Participants in quartile 4, who were the most treatment‐resistant group, receiving nine or more ASMs, showed an unfavorable treatment effect of +15.0% compared with placebo
entries.anchor: Results, Effect on convulsive seizure frequency

entries.proposition: The authors state that lowered plasma 24-hydroxycholesterol confirmed the pharmacological effect.
entries.snippet: Decreased plasma 24HC levels clearly confirmed the pharmacological effect of soticlestat (Figure S2).

entries.proposition: The authors conclude the drug may have modest antiepileptic effects that failed to reach significance.
entries.snippet: The totality of the data from SKYLINE suggests that soticlestat may have modest antiepileptic effects, which failed to achieve statistical significance in patients with DS.

entries.proposition: The study was funded by the manufacturer, and the sponsor does not plan to share data.
entries.snippet: Takeda does not plan to share data supporting the results reported in this article.

entries.proposition: Supplement: median plasma 24HC fell about 80 percent on drug against about 4 percent on placebo.
entries.snippet: By the end of the full treatment period, median plasma 24HC levels had decreased by approximately 80% for soticlestat-treated participants compared with approximately 4% for placebo-treated participants.

entries.proposition: Supplement: no meaningful effect on all-seizure frequency.
entries.snippet: There was no meaningful effect on all-seizure frequency per 28 days for participants receiving soticlestat versus placebo during both the full treatment period and the maintenance period (Table S3).

entries.proposition: Supplement: seizure-free days rose in both arms without a difference.
entries.snippet: Both treatment groups experienced an increase in percentage of seizure-free days, with no meaningful difference between the two groups (Table S3).

entries.proposition: Fig 3: bars are medians with IQR whiskers that overlap widely: placebo -8.64 and soticlestat -22.16 over the full period (n 71 and 73), -11.99 and -23.29 in maintenance (n 68 and 69), -12.70 and -23.34 in the SCN1A-positive subgroup (n 56 and 58).
entries.snippet: [figure attestation - pixels cannot be quote-matched] Fig 3 panels A-C: bars -8.64 versus -22.16 (p = .061), -11.99 versus -23.29 (p = .089), -12.70 versus -23.34 (nominal p = .045); the vertical IQR whisker of each soticlestat bar spans roughly -54 to +23 (A) and every pair of whiskers overlaps; text under the panels gives differences -15.64, -14.29 and -17.38 percent with intervals; panel B maintenance n are 68 and 69.

entries.proposition: Fig 4: the caregiver and clinician global impressions of improvement were 35.3 percent and 26.8 percent on placebo against 60.6 and 52.1 percent on drug; the three non-seizure sub-items were 25.4 versus 25.4, 31.0 versus 32.4 and 19.7 versus 23.9; quality-of-life change was +1.86 on placebo and -1.17 on drug (difference -3.03, nominal p .189).
entries.snippet: [figure attestation - pixels cannot be quote-matched] Fig 4 panels: A responders 9.9 vs 27.4 (nominal p .008); B 11.8 vs 30.4 (.010); C Care GI-I 35.3 vs 60.6 (.004); D CGI-I 26.8 vs 52.1 (.003); E seizure intensity and duration 24.6 vs 58.5 (<.001); F alertness 25.4 vs 25.4 (.741); G communication 31.0 vs 32.4 (.901); H disruptive behaviors 19.7 vs 23.9 (.693); I QI-Disability LS mean change 1.86 (placebo, n 53) vs -1.17 (soticlestat, n 56), difference -3.03 (-7.59 to 1.52), nominal p .189.
